**Answer: No.** The group C\*-algebra $C^*(\mathbb{R}^n)$ does **not** include $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for any $1 \le p \le 2$.

**Proof.**

Since $\mathbb{R}^n$ is an abelian locally compact group, Pontryagin duality identifies its group C\*-algebra with the algebra of continuous functions vanishing at infinity on its dual group:

$$C^*(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\cong\; C_0(\widehat{\mathbb{R}^n}).$$

The dual group of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is again $\mathbb{R}^n$, so

$$C^*(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\cong\; C_0(\mathbb{R}^n).$$

Under this identification, the question "does $C^*(\mathbb{R}^n)$ include $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$?" becomes: is $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) \subseteq C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)$?

This inclusion **fails**. Consider the characteristic function of the unit cube:

$$f = \chi_{[0,1]^n}.$$

This function belongs to $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for every $1 \le p < \infty$ (in particular for $1 \le p \le 2$), since

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |f|^p\,dx = \operatorname{vol}([0,1]^n) = 1 < \infty.$$

However, $f$ is **not continuous** (it has jump discontinuities on the boundary of $[0,1]^n$), and therefore $f \notin C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)$, since $C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)$ consists of continuous functions.

Thus $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) \setminus C_0(\mathbb{R}^n)$, which shows

$$L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\not\subseteq\; C_0(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\cong\; C^*(\mathbb{R}^n)$$

for every $1 \le p \le 2$. $\blacksquare$
